newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: LME copper seen advancing further - Asian trade.
newsitem.headline: LME copper seen advancing further - Asian trade.

text.p: Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are expected to forge ahead on Thursday, but looming concerns about a technical correction could limit a sharp rise in the short term, Far East traders said.
"Copper prices seem to be firm due to a strong close on Wednesday, but the current overbought sentiment will weigh on a further rise," a trader with a local metal house said.
Copper was seen remaining in overbought territory with the 14-day relative strength index (RSI) at 76.14, above the previous day's 73.33.
The market generally considers an RSI of 70 or more as overbought and 30 or less as oversold.
Three-month copper was quoted in thin Asian trade at $2,531/$2,536 a tonne at 0615 GMT, slightly down from Wednesday's late LME close.
Copper prices surged to fresh one-year highs during Wednesday's LME afternoon session, before pulling back to a positive close just above resistance at $2,530.
One trader pegged a resistance for three-month copper at $2,550 and then $2,600. "If copper prices breaches the key resistance of $2,600, we will see a strong bullish market."
He also pegged $2,500 as a key support level.
However, other traders said copper prices were expected to fall slightly or consolidate at current levels for the time being before resuming their rise.
Contrary to the LME's flagship metal, nickel prices were expected to test $7,100 as a key support after falling to $7,250 on Wednesday, prompted by chart-based selling, traders said.

LME broker Macquarie said in its daily report that the main reason for the bearishness was the continued high use of secondary nickel by stainless steel producers, which was believed to have been the result of a build-up of stainless
steel scrap stocks from mid-1995 through to mid-1996.
"We surveyed the main producers yesterday and detected a more bearish mood than a month ago," Macquarie said.
The broker also said there were reports from Europe that stainless steel buyers were cancelling orders previously placed with mills.

Another factor depressing the nickel market over this period was a large rise in nickel exports from Russia, the broker said. "Conversations with traders indicate a 'flood' of material in the fourth quarter of 1996 and the first quarter of this year, perhaps as much as 15,000 tonnes higher than in the
previous quarter, apparently due to de-stocking."

But a trader with POSCO, South Korea's largest steel maker, said even though stalled labour talks at Inco's big Sudbury operation in Canada had been shrugged off on the LME on Wednesday, he expected some support for nickel from this factor as the contract is to expire on May 31.
POSCO buys about 50,000 tonnes of nickel a year, he said.
At 0615 GMT, three-month aluminium prices were bid at $1,641, down $2 a tonne from the previous late LME close.
A regional trader said LME stocks for copper and aluminium are expected to decline further on Thursday.
-- Jae Hur, Seoul Newsroom (822) 727 5651
